lesson_title: The Rondavel Beats the Tin Roof
hook_text: Two houses, one village. One is an oven in January and a fridge in July. The other is comfy all year, with no electricity.
clip_script: The tin-roofed house: thin metal conducts heat straight through. Summer sun bakes it, winter nights drain it. The rondavel next door: a roof of thick thatch, every grass stem a hollow tube full of trapped air. Heat barely gets through. Mud walls soak up heat all day and let it out slowly at night. And the round shape means less wall to lose heat through, while wind slides around it. People designed this centuries ago with what grew and lay nearby. Today architects are copying it: thick walls, insulated roofs, north-facing windows. Old wisdom, new name: energy-efficient design.
visual_style: Whiteboard split of a tin-roofed block house with fast heat arrows and a rondavel with slow, short arrows; a day-and-night thermometer comparison under each.
pacing: Strong contrast up front, a rhythmic tour of the rondavel, a forward-looking finish.
